## NGO Website Development in India: What NPCI's New UPI MDR Rules Mean for Your Donation Checkout

From 15 October 2026, UPI stops being unconditionally free for merchants receiving payments above a certain size, ending a six-year zero-MDR regime that every donation website built in India has quietly relied on. The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced a 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate on eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 per transaction for payments of ₹75,000 and above. For NGO website development in India, this is the first time in years that the UPI donation button — the single most-used donation method on almost every Indian nonprofit's website — has a cost structure attached to it that didn't exist before, and it needs to be understood before donors start asking questions your site isn't ready to answer.

### What the new rule actually says

The framework, as reported across financial and policy coverage in September 2026, breaks down as follows:

- **Person-to-person (P2P) UPI transactions remain completely free**, regardless of amount — this doesn't affect an individual sending money to another individual's personal UPI ID.
- **P2M transactions up to ₹2,000 remain free**, whatever the merchant category.
- **P2M transactions above ₹2,000 attract a 0.4% MDR**, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more.
- **Small merchants and street vendors receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes remain exempt**, continuing under zero MDR as long as they stay under that monthly threshold. A merchant that exceeds ₹1 lakh for three consecutive months moves into the standard P2M category and becomes liable for MDR going forward.
- Select categories — railways, telecom, insurance, fuel — get a flat, reduced MDR of ₹5 per transaction above ₹2,000 rather than the standard 0.4%.
- Capital market transactions (mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers) attract a nominal 0.02% MDR, capped at ₹300.
- Industry reporting estimates roughly 96% of merchant UPI transactions will be unaffected, largely because they fall below the ₹2,000 threshold or qualify for the small-merchant exemption.

### The honest gap: donations aren't explicitly addressed

Here's the part that matters most for an NGO, and where this article has to be direct about the limits of what's confirmed rather than guessing: none of the official NPCI communications or the financial press coverage reviewed for this article specifically names charitable donations, registered trusts, or Section 8 companies as either included in or exempt from the new MDR framework. The published rules classify transactions by amount and by certain named merchant categories (railways, telecom, fuel, capital markets) — donation collection isn't called out as its own category either way.

That means an NGO accepting UPI donations through a payment gateway falls under the general P2M rules by default unless its specific payment aggregator or bank has separately negotiated or confirmed a different treatment. In practice, this comes down to how your NGO's UPI collection is classified with your payment gateway: if a single donation transaction is below ₹2,000, it's unaffected either way; if a donor gives more than ₹2,000 in a single UPI payment, whether that specific transaction now attracts the 0.4% MDR depends on your organisation's registered merchant category code and monthly UPI QR volume, both of which are set by your bank or payment aggregator, not by NPCI directly. TODO: confirm directly with your bank or payment gateway provider whether your NGO's specific merchant registration qualifies for the small-merchant exemption, and get that confirmation in writing rather than assuming either way.

### Why this specifically matters for donation checkouts

Most Indian NGO websites route UPI donations one of two ways: a UPI deep link or QR code generated directly by a payment gateway (Razorpay, Cashfree, Instamojo and similar), or a UPI ID published directly on the donation page for donors to pay to manually. The MDR question plays out differently depending on which model your site uses.

**Gateway-routed UPI donations.** If your donation form generates a payment link through a gateway, that gateway's merchant agreement with your NGO determines your registered category and monthly volume classification — and by extension, whether MDR applies to donations above ₹2,000 processed through it. This is squarely a conversation to have with your gateway provider now, before 15 October, rather than discovering the deduction on a settlement statement afterward.

**Direct UPI ID / QR code donations.** A donation paid directly to a published UPI ID, without going through a merchant gateway, may be treated differently depending on whether that UPI ID is registered as a personal or business/merchant account with the receiving bank — another detail worth confirming directly with your bank rather than assuming a small nonprofit's account defaults to an exempt category.

**Recurring donations via UPI Autopay.** For NGOs running monthly giving programmes through UPI Autopay mandates, the relevant question is whether the per-instalment amount, not the total mandate value, is what's compared against the ₹2,000 threshold. A ₹500-per-month recurring donor mandate would fall well under the threshold on a per-transaction basis even if the annual total is well above it — but this is exactly the kind of detail worth verifying explicitly with your gateway rather than assuming, since a misunderstanding here could mean an unpleasant surprise on settlement reports months into a recurring giving programme.

### How this compares to what NGOs already pay on card and net-banking donations

Context helps here, because a 0.4% figure lands very differently depending on what an organisation is already used to paying elsewhere in its payment stack. Card and net-banking transactions processed through Indian payment gateways have long carried processing fees typically in the 1.5-3% range depending on the gateway, card network and transaction size — a cost most NGOs have already built into their fundraising math without much controversy, because it's simply understood as the price of accepting card payments. Viewed against that baseline, a 0.4% MDR capped at ₹300 on UPI donations above ₹2,000 is a smaller proportional cost than what the same organisation likely already absorbs on its card-based donations, even though it will feel newsworthy specifically because UPI has been free for so long that donors and NGOs alike stopped thinking of it as having any cost at all.

### What to actually check before 15 October 2026

- **Ask your payment gateway directly, in writing, how your NGO's UPI collections are currently classified**, and whether any MDR will apply to donations above ₹2,000 from that date.
- **Check whether your merchant category code reflects your registered nonprofit status accurately.** A misclassified account is one of the more common, avoidable reasons a small organisation ends up paying charges it might otherwise have been exempt from.
- **Review your settlement statements from mid-October onward specifically for MDR deductions**, rather than assuming your existing reconciliation process will automatically flag a new, small percentage-based deduction buried across many transactions.
- **Decide, deliberately, who absorbs any MDR cost** — the organisation, or the donor via a small "cover the transaction fee" checkbox at checkout, which several Indian donation platforms already offer for card and net-banking payments and could reasonably extend to UPI if MDR does apply.
- **Update your donation FAQ page proactively** if MDR does turn out to apply to your organisation's donations above ₹2,000, so a donor checking their bank statement against your stated donation amount isn't left confused by a discrepancy nobody explained to them in advance.

### Why UPI carries so much weight for Indian NGO fundraising specifically

It's worth pausing on why this rule change matters more for an NGO's website than for a typical ecommerce store, even though the underlying framework applies to both equally. Indian nonprofits have leaned on UPI as their default digital donation channel harder than almost any other merchant category, for reasons specific to fundraising: it requires no card details a hesitant first-time donor might be wary of entering, it works from any UPI-enabled banking app most donors already have installed, and it has, until now, been free at every transaction size — a genuinely useful thing to be able to tell a donor when explaining why their entire contribution reaches the cause rather than being reduced by processing fees. That last point is precisely what a modest MDR now complicates, at least for the subset of single donations above ₹2,000, which for many NGOs represents a meaningful share of total donation value even if it's a smaller share of total donation *count* (since large donors tend to give in fewer, bigger transactions than small recurring donors).

### 80G receipts must reflect what the donor actually gave, not what the NGO nets

One compliance detail worth flagging explicitly, because it's easy to get backwards under the pressure of a new fee: an 80G donation receipt must record the amount the donor actually paid, not the amount the NGO received after any gateway or MDR deduction. If a donor pays ₹5,000 via UPI and a portion is deducted as MDR before it reaches your account, the 80G receipt — and any donor-facing thank-you communication — still needs to show ₹5,000 as the donation amount, since that's the figure relevant for the donor's own tax exemption claim under the Income-tax Act. The MDR is a cost the NGO absorbs (or explicitly asks the donor to cover as a separate line item at checkout) — it is not a reduction in the recorded donation amount itself. Getting this backwards, even unintentionally, in an automated receipt-generation system is the kind of small technical bug that can create a real compliance headache for a donor relying on that receipt at tax-filing time, so it's worth explicitly testing your receipt-generation logic against a donation amount above ₹2,000 before the rule takes effect, not after a donor flags a mismatch.

### Don't let this undermine trust in UPI as a donation method

It's worth being clear-eyed about scale here: even in the case where MDR does apply, 0.4% capped at ₹300 is a modest cost relative to the 2-3% typical of card payment processing that many NGOs already absorb without much scrutiny. The bigger risk to an NGO isn't the cost itself — it's an undisclosed, unexplained deduction showing up on reconciliation months from now that erodes trust in your own financial reporting, or a donor whose bank statement shows a slightly different amount than what your receipt confirms, with no explanation on your site for why. Both are avoidable with a short, honest note on your donation page and a five-minute conversation with your payment gateway now, well before the rule takes effect.

### What honest donor communication looks like here

If your NGO does confirm that MDR will apply to donations above ₹2,000 through your gateway, the least useful response is silence, and the least credible response is burying it in fine print nobody reads before donating. A short, plain-language note near your donation amount selector — something like "Donations above ₹2,000 may incur a small payment processing charge of up to 0.4%, in line with NPCI's new UPI merchant rules effective October 2026; your 80G receipt reflects your full donated amount regardless" — does two things at once: it's honest about a real cost, and it pre-empts the exact confusion a donor might otherwise raise after checking their bank statement. Several established Indian donation platforms already display similar processing-fee transparency for card donations; extending the same practice to UPI once (and if) MDR applies is a small addition, not a redesign.

For NGOs offering a "cover the transaction fee" checkbox, this is also a reasonable moment to introduce or extend that option to UPI donations specifically, framed as optional rather than mandatory — donors who choose to cover it are actively opting in to maximise what reaches the cause, while donors who don't are never made to feel they gave less than they intended.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does this affect donations under ₹2,000?**
No — transactions of ₹2,000 or below remain free under the new framework regardless of merchant category, which covers the majority of individual UPI donations most Indian NGOs receive.

**Will donors see a lower amount reach the NGO than what they paid?**
Only if MDR applies to that specific transaction, and even then, standard practice is for the MDR to be deducted from the merchant's settlement rather than added on top of what the donor pays — meaning a donor's bank statement should still show the amount they intended to give, while the NGO may receive slightly less after the gateway's cut. This is a reconciliation and disclosure question for your organisation, not something that should change what a donor is asked to pay at checkout unless you deliberately choose to pass the cost on.

**Should we switch to card payments instead of UPI to avoid this?**
Almost certainly not. Card payment processing in India typically costs more than 0.4% per transaction, and UPI's convenience for Indian donors — no card details, one-tap payment from a banking app already installed — remains a significant conversion advantage regardless of a modest MDR on a subset of transactions. This is a disclosure and reconciliation issue, not a reason to move away from the payment method most Indian donors actually prefer.

**Where can we get an authoritative answer specific to our organisation?**
Your payment gateway's support or relationship team, and your bank if you're also collecting via a directly published UPI ID, are the only sources who can confirm your specific merchant classification and monthly volume status. NPCI's own published FAQs describe the framework in general terms but won't have visibility into how your specific account is categorised.

**Does this change anything about FCRA-registered NGOs receiving foreign donations?**
No — FCRA donations must legally be received into a designated FCRA bank account via specific permitted channels, and typically don't move through the same UPI merchant-collection rails this MDR framework addresses, which governs domestic P2M UPI payments. This rule change is relevant to domestic donation collection specifically; it doesn't alter FCRA's separate foreign-contribution banking requirements.

### Where to go from here

If your NGO's website doesn't currently have a clear, honest note explaining how UPI donations are processed and reconciled, this is a good moment to add one — both as good donor-transparency practice generally and specifically ahead of a rule change that could otherwise show up as an unexplained discrepancy in October's settlement reports. As a team that has built [donation and payment flows](/pages/ngopage) for NGO websites across India, Govindani Infotech helps nonprofits set up UPI, card and Autopay donation checkouts with clear reconciliation and donor-facing disclosure built in from the start — [contact us](/contact-us) if you'd like your current donation checkout reviewed ahead of the October changeover.

Donors will have questions once this shows up in their bank SMS or the checkout screen, and that's a conversation many NGOs now handle over WhatsApp rather than email — which raises a related question worth thinking through at the same time: [whether an AI agent on your WhatsApp donor line is ready to field that kind of question accurately](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-whatsapp-business-agent-2026), or whether it belongs with a human until the framework settles.
